doc.title: Christine Jensen interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 4, 2024

title: Directing soloists, and the story behind Nishiyuu
summary: She explains that she tells the band why she wrote a piece, such as Nishiyuu on Habitat, inspired by a march of northern youth for clean drinking water.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: Have you ever had an experience — you wrote glowingly about people that you work with, the soloists and so forth. I wonder if you’ve ever had a semi-awkward experience where people were interpreting your music during their solos in a fashion that didn’t really ring for you, and as the composer have you had to say, “Could you consider a different approach to this?”

Yeah that happens all the time I think. I might, you know, if I write something new and I throw it down in front of the band, this is a large ensemble. It’s a little different than small ensemble. If I’m in a quartet I can freely go crazy with my thoughts with the band because there’s only three or four of them in the room with me. But when you get to the hierarchy of placing a big band together there’s like little leadership roles going on everywhere. Right? So lead trumpet players are different everywhere. Drummers are different everywhere. So I might have to get into things more with certain players depending on the situation. With my own band if I’m writing something new and it’s not really connecting I might just stop and talk about what I wrote about and why I wrote it, and that tends to put the whole thing back together. So for example “Nishiyuu” on “Habitat” came — I wrote that because I had been probably sitting in my office doing work or writing, and every day on the CBC the news came on about this certain tribe up north beyond Hudson Bay up on the east side of Hudson Bay — do you know how far away that is? That’s very, very, very far away. It’s like 3000 kilometers or something. And they’re sitting up there, this tribe of — a young group of people from the community, and they’re like we have no drinking water and we need to send a message to the government about how our drinking water is not clean. We live in Canada. Every person should have the right to clean drinking water. And they went on this march. So I hadn’t told anyone this, they didn’t know what Nishiyuu was. I’m like you know this is actually a branch off the Cree tribe that is going to march through the most miserable conditions in the world of weather from north to south from January to March to Parliament Hill so they meet at the right time with the Prime Minister and blah blah. So anyway I have to tell this story and I was practically in tears over it, and then they played it so beautifully. You know what I mean? But they didn’t know what Nishiyuu was, they didn’t know anything until I sat down, and I think I pulled a Globe and Mail article on it and I gave it to my soloist. I said, “You know what? Just read this and it’ll all make sense. You’re my leader on this piece.” And ever since I just love playing that.
